Cowork = autonomous execution for general knowledge work. Code = autonomous execution specifically for software projects. Same underlying agentic capability, different audiences and file types.

sectionTitle: The folder-permission model
text: Cowork doesn't get free rein over your entire computer. It operates through a folder-permission model: you explicitly grant it read, write, and create access to specific directories, and it works within that boundary. 1 You choose the folder Point Cowork at a specific directory — not your whole file system — where the relevant files for the task actually live. 2 You describe the task In plain language — "organize these invoices into a spreadsheet," "summarize these meeting notes into one document." 3 It plans and executes autonomously Within that granted folder, it reads files, creates new ones, and organizes content — without needing you to approve each individual action along the way. 💡 Why the scoping matters: Granting access to one project folder rather than your entire Documents directory limits the blast radius if something goes wrong — the same principle as giving someone a key to one room rather than the whole building.

sectionTitle: The kind of work Cowork is actually built for
text: Concrete examples make this land better than the abstract description: 🧾 Turning invoices into a spreadsheet Point it at a folder of PDF invoices and ask for a formatted spreadsheet with the totals extracted — Cowork reads each file and builds the working output. 📝 Consolidating scattered notes into one document A folder of loose meeting notes becomes a single, organized summary document, without you manually piecing it together. 📊 Pulling metrics into a formatted report Gathering scattered figures into one coherent, presentable report — the kind of task that's simple in concept but tedious to assemble by hand. 🗂️ Organizing a messy folder by content Sorting files based on what's actually inside them, not just filenames — something that requires actually reading each file to do well. 💡 The common thread: Every one of these tasks involves real files, multiple steps, and a defined outcome — exactly the shape of work that benefits from delegation rather than a single conversational answer.

sectionTitle: A real incident worth knowing about
text: Being clear-eyed about risk makes a tool more useful, not less. One documented example is worth understanding directly: early user reports described a case where Cowork consumed a large volume of files (reported as around 11GB) during testing, unintentionally. ⚠️ Why this happened, most likely: Cowork operates with real read/write/create access within its granted folder and works autonomously — meaning a misunderstood instruction or an edge case in a task can result in real, unintended changes to real files, not just a wrong text answer you can simply disregard. This connects directly to Module 5's trust-boundary framework: reading files is low-risk and reversible. But writing, overwriting, or deleting files is a different category — those actions have real, sometimes hard-to-reverse consequences, which is exactly why backup practices matter here in a way they don't for a purely conversational tool. Low risk Reading and analyzing files Reversible by nature — nothing is altered. Medium-to-high risk Creating, modifying, or reorganizing files Real changes to real data. Worth having backups before granting broad access, especially for a new or unfamiliar task.

sectionTitle: Design a safe first task
text: You want to try Cowork for the first time, on a folder of 50 old project files you don't fully remember the contents of. Using what you've learned about the folder-permission model and honest risks, describe how you'd set up this first task responsibly.

sectionTitle: Practical habits for staying in control
text: None of the risk above means avoiding Cowork — it means using it with the same reasonable caution you'd apply to any tool with real access to your files. A few concrete habits: 💾 Back up before granting access to anything important Especially for a new or unfamiliar type of task — a backup turns a potential disaster into a minor inconvenience. 🔍 Scope folder access narrowly Grant access to the specific project folder the task needs, not a broad parent directory "just in case." 🏢 In a workplace setting, governance is a real responsibility Anthropic itself has been clear that while some oversight tooling exists, organizations rolling out Cowork broadly are responsible for their own governance and controls — this isn't something to assume is fully handled for you. ✅ Review results before treating them as final Especially early on, or for anything consequential — the same "verify before you fully trust" habit from Module 7's discussion of AI reliability. 💡 The mindset that ties it together: Cowork's power comes from autonomous, real-world file access — which is exactly why the same care that applies to any powerful tool with real consequences applies here too.
